title: Most of the estimated rain-slope loss remained after seasonal covariance adjustment in 175 south-east Australian catchments
abstract: We test whether changed seasonal rain covariance can explain the reported loss of annual rain sensitivity after 1997. We use 175 source-selected south-east Australian catchments, calendar years 1951-2021, and AGCD and SILO rain. An exact projection identity separates the annual slope change into changed seasonal slopes and changed seasonal covariance weights. For 2010-2021, annual slope losses are 27.1% and 21.6%. Two seasonal groups give positive rain-mix terms of 2.7 and 2.1 percentage points, which offset the loss. Four-quarter fits give mix terms of -6.7 and -7.6 points, leaving 75% and 65% of the point loss within seasonal slopes. For 1997-2021, four-quarter fits leave 79% and 76%. Shared year and cell resampling gives negative response ranges in both products. Ordinary row resampling often loses rank, so an added positive-weight method retains all observed years. We report both methods and their limits. Independent scalar fits and fixed-response tests verify the identity and code. This is a statistical constraint, not physical attribution. Nonlinear weather response, shared rain errors, short eras, source selection and approximate uncertainty remain limits. Code, hashes, aggregate draws, figures and reproduction instructions are supplied.

display.caption: Annual slope change and its exact response and seasonal rain-mix terms. Two groups and four quarters; 175 catchments; 2010-2021 against 1951-1996. Bars show 95% positive-block ranges with three-year blocks and cell weights. These ranges do not have established exact confidence coverage.
Response and rain-mix ranges under two year-weight methods and 1-, 3-, 5-year blocks. Ordinary row ranges condition on valid rank. Both methods include spatial cell weights and refit both eras.
